title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data

paper.title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
paper.abstract: Abstract Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering , which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model’s own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B’s training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Ensuring that large language models (LLMs) help with benign requests while refusing harmful ones remains central to safe deployment. Activation steering controls this behavior at inference time by modifying internal representations without updating model parameters. A single direction can substantially alter refusal behavior Arditi et al. (2024) , making steering useful for behavioral control and probing learned safety mechanisms. Identifying a reliable direction is therefore crucial. A common approach constructs a steering set of positive and negative examples. Contrastive activation addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) and difference-of-means refusal steering Arditi et al. (2024) subtract the mean negative activations from the mean positive activations to obtain a single steering direction. However, these directions can have variable effects across inputs, fail under prompt changes, or reverse the intended behavior through anti-steering Tan et al. (2024) ; Braun et al. (2025) . This raises a fundamental question: which contrastive examples should define the steering direction? In this paper, we introduce genesis steering , which constructs steering directions from contrastive examples in the model’s own fine-tuning data. We term these examples genesis data and their difference-of-means direction a genesis vector . Since fine-tuning data shapes the model’s refusal and compliance behavior, it provides a natural reference for steering. We focus on refusal, for which safety fine-tuning data often contain both harmful requests paired with refusals and benign requests paired with compliant responses. This contrastive structure allows us to derive both classes directly from the data. However, fine-tuning datasets are not always publicly released or fully documented, limiting direct access to genesis data. To address this limitation, we extend genesis steering using membership inference queries , originally developed to estimate whether an example was used during training Shokri et al. (2017) ; Fu et al. (2024) . Given a dedicated steering set, we rank examples by their membership scores, retain likely training examples, and compute a proxy genesis vector from their positive and negative activation means. This approach uses membership inference to curate dataset rather than requiring access to the original fine-tuning data. Its effectiveness depends on whether the scores identify examples that reflect the model’s actual training data. We provide two theoretical results supporting this approach. First, We draw on recent Mahalanobis-based out-of-distribution (OoD) detection in learned LLM representations Liu et al. (2024) ; Feng et al. (2026) ; Barkley et al. (2026) , and prove that under specific distributional assumptions, the genesis vector minimizes the Euclidean displacement needed to reach the decision boundary (see Section 3.2 ). Second, under a mixture model with mean-preserving selection, we prove that membership-based proxies reduce the class-mean estimation bias when the true positive rate exceeds the false positive rate. When both classes share the mixture proportion and detection rates, the same reduction applies to steering-vector bias. We first evaluate genesis steering on Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, comparing vectors constructed from seven safety datasets and one contrastive split from the CAA datasets Rimsky et al. (2024) . At layer 16 16 , we measure how far each vector moves the model toward compliance across five benchmarks: HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) , StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) , XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) , OR-Bench ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , and Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) . We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B’s training mixture yield stronger steering vectors than the external datasets considered, on both models, even though Llama-3.1-8B-Instructwas not trained on any of these datasets. This result highlights the importance of the choice of steering data, beyond the choice of steering method alone. We next evaluate whether membership inference can recover this advantage when the original fine-tuning data are unavailable. Using 10 10 membership scores, we construct genesis proxy datasets for both models and examine the resulting steering vectors. On Tülu-3-8B, the scores largely agree in ranking examples, preferentially identify its fine-tuning data, and produce vectors that outperform those built from bottom-ranked examples while remaining competitive with random subsets of the same size. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the scores disagree, and top-ranked examples yield worse steering than random selection. These findings suggest that MIA methods will only have a positive effect if shifting the mean with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than shifting the mean with OoD data.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our main contributions may be summarized as follows: • We introduce genesis steering, which constructs steering vectors from a model’s own contrastive fine-tuning data, and extend it with membership inference to construct proxy datasets when the original data are unavailable. • We establish theoretical guarantees for optimal boundary-reaching directions and reduced proxy-estimation bias under explicit distributional and selection assumptions. • We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, showing that model-specific fine-tuning data can improve steering and that membership-based selection can recover this benefit when the candidate pool contains the model’s actual training examples.

sections.heading: Activation steering methods.
sections.text: The linear representation hypothesis relates concept directions in activation space to model steering Park et al. (2024) . Activation addition Turner et al. (2024) and contrastive activation addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) construct directions from activation differences, while other methods intervene on attention heads Li et al. (2023) , sparse autoencoder features O’Brien et al. (2025) , optimized vectors Cao et al. (2024) , or activation rotations Vu and Nguyen (2025) . Broader frameworks include representation engineering and context dependent vector fields Zou et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2026) . Because these interventions act at inference time, they adjust a deployed model’s behaviour without retraining it or changing its weights. Comparative studies emphasize the importance of simple baselines Wu et al. (2025) ; Im and Li (2026) . We focus on the data used to estimate a direction within the difference-of-means framework, formalized in Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: Refusal geometry and steering data.
sections.text: A single direction can substantially control refusal Arditi et al. (2024) , although recent work finds multiple refusal directions and richer geometric structure Joad et al. (2026) ; Wollschläger et al. (2025) . Refusal and harmfulness can also be represented separately Zhao et al. (2025) , while post-training affects refusal circuits and their steerability Nguyen et al. (2026) . More directly, the reliability of an extracted direction depends on the contrastive dataset, on prompt design Tan et al. (2024) ; Braun et al. (2025) and on the activations it is read from Ye et al. (2026) ; separation between positive and negative pools and consistency of activation differences predict steerability Braun et al. (2025) . Contrastive vectors can also entangle refusal with style and capabilities Cristofano (2026) or interfere across attributes Nguyen et al. (2025) ; Gao et al. (2026) . Closest to our setting, persona vectors run the reverse direction, projecting candidate training data onto a trait direction to flag data that will shift behaviour Chen et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; we instead estimate the direction from the training data. Genesis steering addresses this dependence on reference data by using the model’s own fine-tuning examples. Section 3.2 establishes population-level optimality under explicit assumptions.

sections.heading: Membership inference for genesis steering.
sections.text: Membership inference is traditionally studied as a privacy attack for determining whether a candidate example was used in training Shokri et al. (2017) . For language models, attacks have been studied in masked model and fine-tuning settings Mireshghallah et al. (2022) ; Fu et al. (2024) , using neighborhood comparisons Mattern et al. (2023) and relative conditional likelihoods Xie et al. (2024) . Their reliability depends on the evaluation setting, and distribution shifts between members and non members can confound apparent success Duan et al. (2024) ; Meeus et al. (2025) . In our setting, membership scores are instead used to select proxy genesis data from an available steering set.

At inference, the intervention h ℓ ′ = h ℓ + α ​ v ℓ ​ ( D ) h^{\prime}_{\ell}=h_{\ell}+\alpha v_{\ell}(D) is applied at the chosen token positions. The signed coefficient α \alpha controls its strength and orientation: positive values are intended to promote the positive class and negative values the negative class. This changes the source of the steering dataset while retaining the intervention rule. Section 3.2 analyzes the population counterpart of this estimator; Section 3.3 constructs a proxy and analyzes its bias when the fine-tuning data is unavailable.

( 1 ). In this section, “more effective” refers to a direction that requires a smaller Euclidean displacement to cross the linear boundary between the positive and negative regions. Mahalanobis-based OoD detection has been studied for Transformer encoders Podolskiy et al. (2021) ; Zhou et al. (2021) and LLM representations Liu et al. (2024) . sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments address three questions: whether a model’s own fine-tuning datasets steer it better than external ones (§ 4.1 ), which pair (prompt, response) are ranked high by a membership score s ⁡ ( x ) s(x) and why (§ 4.2 – 4.3 ), and how the selected vectors steer (§ 4.4 ).

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: Both models share the Llama-3.1-8B base ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . Tülu-3-8B ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) is post-trained on a public SFT mixture, whereas Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct uses undisclosed data ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . We use Tülu-3-8B to study membership selection when training membership is known and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a negative control; none of the datasets considered here is known to overlap with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct’s post-training data. Membership scores are computed using the Tülu-3-8B SFT checkpoint, while activations and steering use the final Tülu-3-8B model. Some methods additionally use the Llama-3.1-8B base model or a Tülu-3-8B SFT model trained without the safety data, called the twin . Each model uses its own chat template.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We split each dataset into refusal and compliance poles according to its gold responses (Appendix C ). Three datasets belong to Tülu-3-8B’s SFT mixture (marked † \dagger ): CoCoNot safety requests (CCN) ( Brahman et al., 2024 ) , WildJailbreak (WJB) ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) , and WildGuardMix (WGM) ( Han et al., 2024 ) . Together, they contain approximately 111k of the mixture’s 939k prompts and constitute Tülu-3-8B’s genesis data . External datasets are CoCoNot rows excluded from the mixture (CCN-out), Do-Not-Answer (DNA) ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , HH-RLHF (HH) ( Bai et al., 2022 ) , and PKU-SafeRLHF (PKU) ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . We also use 393 393 refusal pairs from CAA ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , whose responses were authored by the dataset creators. CAA provides a stylistically distinct comparison and has previously yielded vectors with inconsistent steering across inputs ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Braun et al., 2025 ) . We use CAA solely as a ’bad’ comparison for the membership separability experiments. We do not use in other experiments. Details are given in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Membership inference methods.
sections.text: Scores are computed on response tokens conditioned on the prompt, with higher values indicating greater likelihood of membership. We use 10 10 methods on Tülu-3-8B and 9 9 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Appendix D ); one method is unavailable for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as it requires a twin model. Loss, zlib, Min-K%, and Min-K%++ use response likelihood ( Carlini et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) ; gap scores measure agreement with the model’s next-token predictions; and ReCaLL, s base s_{\text{base}} , and s twin s_{\text{twin}} compare the target with a reference model or prefix prompt ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Watson et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: Selection and steering protocol.
sections.text: For each membership method, we rank examples by their scores and select the highest-scoring examples to construct a proxy genesis dataset. We then divide the selected examples into refusal and compliance poles according to their gold responses. Provided both poles are nonempty, we compute the steering vector as the difference between their mean activations at the input of layer 16 16 , using the last prompt token (Eq. 1 ). We evaluate each vector across multiple values of the steering dose α \alpha .

sections.heading: Steerability.
sections.text: A vector flips a prompt if some dose α \alpha gives a non-degenerate response with the benchmark’s target label, compliance on harmful prompts and refusal on benign ones. Its range r b ​ ( v ) r_{b}(v) on benchmark b b is the share of flipped prompts among those P b P_{b} not already at the target unsteered, and its steerability averages the two directions, S ⁡ ( v ) = 1 2 ​ | B h | ​ ∑ b ∈ B h r b ​ ( v ) + 1 2 ​ | B s | ​ ∑ b ∈ B s r b ​ ( v ) , \hskip-8.0ptS(v)=\frac{1}{2|B_{h}|}\sum_{b\in B_{h}}r_{b}(v)+\frac{1}{2|B_{s}|}\sum_{b\in B_{s}}r_{b}(v), (11) over the harmful benchmarks B h B_{h} and the benign ones B s B_{s} . Both directions are weighted equally, so a vector scores high only if it moves the model in both directions. Section 4.1 gives the protocol.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Each of the seven datasets yields one vector, computed from a seeded draw of 128 refusal and 128 compliance examples from its respective poles (Appendix C ). Each vector is normalized and applied at the input of layer 16, at the last prompt token and every generated token. We subtract it on harmful benchmarks (HarmBench and StrongREJECT) and add it on benign benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench, and Alpaca). Responses are evaluated by the LLM judge gemma-2-27b-it (Appendix E.3 ). We evaluate each prompt at every whole-number dose, covering the original ranges ( | α | ≤ 12 |\alpha|\leq 12 for harmful and | α | ≤ 8 |\alpha|\leq 8 for benign benchmarks; Appendix E.4 ), to determine whether a vector flips the prompt at any tested dose rather than identify the optimal α \alpha . We report the range, the steerability S S , the share of prompts lost to degeneration (i.e., those that degenerate at some dose), and the median lowest flipping dose. On Tülu-3-8B, the three datasets from its SFT mixture yield genesis vectors, while the other four yield external vectors. Since none of the seven datasets is known to belong to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct’s post-training data, the same comparison serves as a control for whether an advantage is associated with training on the selected data. sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 1 compares the steerability of the seven datasets. On Tülu-3-8B, genesis vectors reach 0.924–0.990, compared with 0.730–0.977 for external vectors. WildGuardMix performs best, although external HH-RLHF comes close, and CoCoNot performs similarly to its held-out rows. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct shows the same ordering. The mean steerability is higher for genesis than for external datasets on both models, with a lower difference on Tülu-3-8B ( − - 0.024 ± \pm 0.012 from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Overall, the mixture’s datasets provide strong steering vectors across both models, suggesting that their effectiveness extends beyond the model on which they were used for training. Sections 4.2 – 4.4 examine whether membership-based selection improves steering within each dataset.

sections.heading: 4.2 Membership inference ranking
sections.text: Figure 1: (a) Mean membership scores for each dataset, in pooled-pole standard deviations; further right means more member-like. Bars span scores, filled symbols show medians, and open symbols show s base s_{\text{base}} . (b, c) AUCs for separating Tülu-3-8B’s SFT mixture from other data, with bootstrap standard errors (1000 resamples). Dotted lines indicate chance and solid lines response-length separation. Full values are in Tables 6 and 8 . Figure 1 a shows the membership score distributions for each dataset and pole, with scores standardised across the pooled refusal and compliance examples. For refusal examples, the ordering is largely consistent across models: the three datasets in Tülu-3-8B’s SFT mixture score above the pooled mean, whereas CAA’s authored responses and HH-RLHF, whose responses were generated by an earlier assistant model, score below it for all methods except s base s_{\text{base}} .

sections.heading: Authored answers fall to the bottom.
sections.text: CAA accounts for 0.065 of the pooled refusal pole, but falls in the bottom 0.088–0.188 quartile for every score on both models (Appendix Table 9 ). Score-based selection therefore removes CAA examples disproportionately. Both CAA poles fall below the pool mean for every likelihood score (refusals − - 1.147 to − - 0.294; compliances − - 1.300 to − - 0.744 on Tülu-3-8B). The CAA responses are over all not designed to follow SFT-like patterns but explicitly to evoke steering contrast. Specifically, the compliance examples fall further because some answer harmful requests or speak as a human, unlike aligned assistant responses (“As an AI system, I do not consume substances”).

sections.heading: Training data compared to external data.
sections.text: Figure 1 b,c shows the scores’ AUC on the separation between Tülu-3-8B’s SFT mixture and external data. On the pooled refusal pole, all scores achieve high AUC for Tülu-3-8B (0.848–0.970), and moderately high for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct(0.662–0.878). Compared to response length score (reaching 0.813), scores outperform on Tülu-3-8B, but are comparable on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. On the compliance pole, both models’ scores outperform the length score, while having an even greater separability. After regressing out the four model-independent features (response and prompt length, zlib ratio, and refusal-opening register, scoring up to 0.876), we find that the residual scores still separate the polled on both models, though much less on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (see Appendix E.1 ). Separation may be explained partly by source and response style, though the gap between the two models indicates an additional training-related effect. Once source and response style are matched, membership inference approaches chance (WildGuardMix AUC– 0.516–0.540) whenever distribution shifts are removed ( Duan et al., 2024 ; Meeus et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Selection.
sections.text: Across sources, membership scores rank examples whose responses resemble the target model’s outputs more highly. On Tülu-3-8B, this also prioritizes its alignment data, including its genesis data. We therefore use the scores to select examples representative of the model’s alignment data, rather than as reliable indicators of individual membership.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 3 resports the steerability of each vector. On Tülu-3-8B, every over-refusal steerability reach near perfect score (0.983 to 1.000), while jailbreak shows more variability, amounting therefore for the variability of the overall steerability S S . The Tülu-3-8B’s genesis vector being built mostly from its genesis data (as per membership agreement, Section 4.3 ), reaches higher steerability than random subsets of the same size. Compared prompt by prompt, their steerability S S is + + 0.009 to + + 0.014 higher (Gap: + + 0.014, 95% interval − - 0.001 to + + 0.029), and for every score the top selection steers better than the bottom one ( + + 0.007 to + + 0.033). On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, for which the same subsets are not genesis data, the steerability is worse than random subsets ( − - 0.454 to − - 0.058), and top-consensus membership proxy usually damages the steerability. This matches the intuition of Proposition 1 where optimal displacement is subject to the size of the mean direction shift under MIA-filtered in-distribution data. This additionally indicates that membership selection reduces separation between the poles, and reduces steerability ( Braun et al., 2025 ) (see Appendix E.2 ). Table 3 also reports the prompts lost to degeneration. On Tülu-3-8B, the lost share remains below 0.047, whereas it reaches 0.409 for Min-K%++’s top selection on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. This again hints at a stronger displacement on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct than on Tülu-3-8B, showing the importance of distribution shifts in steerability. When the shift is controlled, a proxy genesis vector is thus as least as strong as a random subset where the candidate pool holds the model’s genesis data.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced genesis steering, which derives steering directions from a model’s own fine-tuning data, and studied membership inference as a means of constructing proxy datasets when the data is unavailable. Our experiments show that the choice of reference data matters: safety data from Tülu-3-8B’s training mixture yield effective steering vectors on both Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Membership-based selection preferentially recovers Tülu-3-8B’s fine-tuning data and produces competitive steering vectors, whereas it does not provide the same benefit on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, where the candidate data are unlikely to belong to its training set. These results support membership inference as a practical tool for proxy construction when the candidate pool contains relevant training examples, while highlighting the importance of evaluating selection through downstream steering. More broadly, they suggest that the composition of safety fine-tuning data shapes the directions available for steering. Understanding how training-data composition affects these directions may help guide the design of both fine-tuning mixtures and steering methods.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: Our experiments cover two 8B models sharing the Llama-3.1-8B base, one steering layer and position, and seven English safety datasets. The results may differ across architectures, scales, layers, languages, and steering tasks. We also study only difference-of-means steering. Whether genesis-based selection benefits methods that optimize steering vectors directly ( Cao et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) remains open. Membership ground truth is available for Tülu-3-8B but not for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which serves as a negative control. Within a single data source, our membership analysis is limited to WildGuardMix, where members and non-members share a response generator. Broader validation therefore depends on access to fine-tuning data from additional models. Finally, we study refusal steering, whose contrastive classes can be derived directly from safety data. Other attributes, such as sycophancy, verbosity, and persona, may require constructing the contrastive split and could interact with refusal steering ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . Our evaluation also relies on a single LLM judge (gemma-2-27b-it) and fixed decoding settings; reported standard errors capture prompt-sampling variability but not judge error or decoding variability.

sections.heading: 7 Potential Risks and Ethics Statements
sections.text: Steering can weaken a model’s refusals as well as strengthen them: the same vectors that induce refusal of benign requests also make the models comply with harmful ones. We study this to understand where refusal behavior comes from and how reliably it can be controlled, not to provide a jailbreak. activation steering requires white-box access to the model, and the directions we use are simple differences of means that are already known to work. We do not release model responses to harmful prompts. Where the appendix shows examples of compliance with a harmful request, it shows only the first sentence. All models and datasets are public and are used under their licenses. The harmful prompts come from public safety benchmarks. Membership inference could in principle be used to probe a model for its training data. For these models and scores, we find that individual training examples are detected only weakly, and not at all where members and non-members share a source and a response generator.

sections.heading: Membership scores and proxy quality.
sections.text: Our results show that membership scores do not necessarily translate into better steering vectors. On Tülu-3-8B, top-ranked examples yield vectors competitive with random subsets of the same size, whereas on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct they yield worse steering. This difference is consistent with the fact that membership-based selection is useful only insofar as the candidate pool contains examples relevant to the model’s fine-tuning data. However, membership alone may not explain the observed differences in steering performance. In particular, safety datasets can differ in response length, style, and register between refusal and compliance examples. Membership scores may partly reflect these distributional properties, which can affect the selected class means even when the scores identify training examples overall. Moreover, selection may affect the two classes differently: a shift in either class mean changes the difference-of-means vector, and unequal shifts need not improve its direction. This provides a possible explanation for why membership-based selection can identify relevant examples without consistently improving downstream steering. These observations also clarify the scope of our theoretical result. The bias reduction guarantee relies on assumptions about the selection mechanism and the activation distributions. In practice, membership scores induce a data-dependent selection that may violate these assumptions, and reduced class-mean bias does not by itself guarantee improved steering performance. Future work could investigate this gap by measuring selection rates and activation-mean shifts separately for each class, and by controlling for observable features such as response length and style.

sections.heading: Implications for fine-tuning data design.
sections.text: Table 4: Number of examples per pole, as used by the membership scores (Section 4 ). The column In SFT says whether the pole’s examples are in Tülu-3-8B’s SFT mixture, and the column Response says where the gold response comes from. dataset refusal compliance refusal in SFT compliance in SFT response WildGuardMix † 1000 1000 yes yes the dataset’s response WildJailbreak † 1000 1000 yes yes the dataset’s response CoCoNot † 1000 471 yes no the dataset’s response CoCoNot, left out 175 – no – the dataset’s response Do-Not-Answer 715 155 no no GPT-4’s recorded response HH-RLHF 1000 1000 no no the chosen response PKU-SafeRLHF 734 1000 no no a response labelled safe CAA 393 393 no no written by the dataset authors The results also suggest that the composition of fine-tuning data may influence the effectiveness of activation steering. If a model’s training examples define useful contrastive directions in its representation space, then the balance, diversity, and consistency of these examples may affect the resulting steering vector. This raises the possibility of designing fine-tuning mixtures not only for the behavior they teach, but also for how reliably that behavior can be controlled at inference time. Testing this possibility requires separating the effect of data composition from differences in model behavior and training procedure. For example, one could vary the balance and diversity of contrastive examples while holding the training setup fixed, then measure both task performance and the stability of the resulting steering directions across prompts and benchmarks. Whether such choices improve steerability without weakening other safety properties remains an open question.

sections.heading: Appendix C Datasets and Poles
sections.text: Table 4 provide datasets sizes, poles and response type.

sections.heading: Pole rule.
sections.text: An example’s pole is decided from its gold response. It is considered a refusal if the response opens as a refusal and a compliance if the response answers with no refusal or deflection language in its first 300 characters. Other examples are dropped. Prompts are kept if they have 12–3,000 characters, at least 95% of them ASCII. Duplicates are removed, and each pole is shuffled with a fixed seed and capped at 1,000 examples. Steering vectors of single datasets use a seeded draw of 128 examples per pole.

sections.heading: Sources.
sections.text: WildJailbreak and WildGuardMix rows are kept only where the dataset’s harm label agrees with the pole. CoCoNot’s refusal pole is its requests with safety concerns subset as it appears in Tülu-3-8B’s mixture. Its compliance pole comes from CoCoNot’s contrast and preference sets, which are not in the mixture. “CoCoNot, left out” holds the safety rows of CoCoNot’s release that the mixture does not contain; it has no compliance pole of its own. HH-RLHF refusals come from the harmless-base split and compliances from the helpful-base split. CAA is the generated split of the refusal behavior, duplicated by question. Each question has two authored answers, one for each pole. sections.heading: Appendix D Membership Scores
sections.text: Let x x be a prompt and y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) the gold response. A model M M reads ( x , y ) (x,y) in its chat template, and ℓ t M = log ⁡ p M ​ ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) \ell_{t}^{M}=\log p_{M}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) is the log-probability of the t t -th response token, the closing end-of-turn token included. Let p M ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) p_{M}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) be the full next-token distribution, μ t \mu_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} the mean and standard deviation of log ⁡ p M ​ ( v ∣ x , y < t ) \log p_{M}(v\mid x,y_{<t}) over the vocabulary under that distribution, and y ^ t = arg ⁡ max v ​ p M ​ ( v ∣ x , y < t ) \hat{y}_{t}=\arg\max_{v}p_{M}(v\mid x,y_{<t}) the model’s own choice. For a set of values, low k \operatorname{low}_{k} denotes the mean of its k = 20 % k=20\% smallest elements. Every score is oriented so that larger means more member-like. The target is Tülu-3-8B-SFT for Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for itself.

sections.heading: Likelihood of the response.
sections.text: • Loss : 1 T ​ ∑ t ℓ t \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\ell_{t} , the negative mean token loss. • zlib ( Carlini et al., 2021 ) : ∑ t ℓ t \sum_{t}\ell_{t} divided by the length in bytes of the zlib-compressed response. Text that compresses well, and is therefore predictable for reasons unrelated to the model, is discounted. • Min-K% ( Shi et al., 2024 ) : low k ⁡ ( { ℓ t } ) \operatorname{low}_{k}(\{\ell_{t}\}) , the mean over the least likely 20% of tokens. A member is expected to contain few very unlikely tokens. • Min-K%++ ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) : low k ⁡ ( { ( ℓ t − μ t ) / σ t } ) \operatorname{low}_{k}(\{(\ell_{t}-\mu_{t})/\sigma_{t}\}) , each token’s log-probability standardised by the model’s own distribution at that position. A training example is expected to sit near a local maximum of the likelihood.

sections.heading: Agreement with the model’s own choice.
sections.text: • Gap : 1 T ​ ∑ t ( ℓ t − log ⁡ p M ​ ( y ^ t ∣ x , y < t ) ) ≤ 0 \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\big(\ell_{t}-\log p_{M}(\hat{y}_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\big)\leq 0 , the mean distance between the gold token and the token the model prefers; zero when the response is the model’s greedy continuation. • Min-K gap : low k \operatorname{low}_{k} of the same per-token gaps. • Top-1 : the share of positions with y t = y ^ t y_{t}=\hat{y}_{t} .

sections.heading: Scores relative to a reference.
sections.text: • ReCaLL ( Xie et al., 2024 ) : the ratio of the response’s mean log-likelihood behind a fixed prefix of ten non-member conversations (HH-RLHF, in the target’s template) to its mean log-likelihood without it. A member’s likelihood is expected to drop more when non-member context is prepended. • s base s_{\text{base}} ( Carlini et al., 2021 ; Watson et al., 2022 ) : the target’s mean log-likelihood minus that of the Llama-3.1-8B base model, both in the target’s template. The base model calibrates for how predictable the text is before post-training. • s twin s_{\text{twin}} (Tülu-3-8B only): the mean log-likelihood under Tülu-3-8B-SFT minus that under the twin trained on the same mixture without its safety data. The two models differ only in the safety data, so s twin s_{\text{twin}} is the reference-calibrated score closest to a controlled experiment.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: Scoring requires one forward pass per example and model in bfloat16. The response is every token after the chat template’s generation prompt. For ReCaLL, the prefix’s key–value cache is computed once and reused; on the first batch, the cached and uncached log-probabilities agreed with each other to within 0.1 on every token. Part 3, mia_panel.py .

sections.heading: The Min-K%++ outlier on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
sections.text: The largest loss, Min-K%++’s top selection on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( S S 0.489, jailbreak range 0.292, 0.409 of prompts lost to degeneration), is the extreme case of an unequal pole shift (see Section E.2 ). Min-K%++ is the weakest of the three selection scores on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (AUC 0.709 on refusals), and what it ranks highest differs between the poles: WildJailbreak supplies 29/74 of the refusal / compliance examples and CoCoNot 41/5, so the difference of means also contrasts sources. Its vector has a cosine of 0.646 to the whole pool’s, against 0.822–0.918 for the other selections and 0.972 for the random draws. Gap and consensus show the same skew in milder form (WildJailbreak 70/99 and 39/70) and lose less. On Tülu-3-8B, selections turned as far from the pool (down to 0.814) steer as well as random, so the turn alone does not explain the loss on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

sections.heading: E.2 How Membership Scoring Shapes the Steering Vector
sections.text: Figure 4: Within each dataset, a score selects the top and the bottom third of each pole, at the input of block 16 (last prompt token), and each model ranks by its own scores. (a) The cosine between the selected vector and the whole pool’s, averaged over the six datasets with both poles. The shaded band is the range a random third reaches, from its 2.5% quantile to 1. (b) How far the top third lies from the bottom third along the pool’s refusal–compliance axis, in pooled standard deviations, for the refusal pole (filled) and the compliance pole (open), averaged over the same datasets. A selection that preserved the means would leave both poles at zero, and one that treated the poles alike would move them equally. Table 15 gives the values. Proposition 2 assumes that selection preserves the mean of each mixture component and treats both poles alike. We test this directly. Within each dataset, the top and the bottom third of each pole by a membership score form two vectors, which we compare with the vector of the whole pool and with 50 randomly sampled thirds, at the input of block 16, on each model (see Figure 4 ). A random third reproduces the pool’s direction (median cosine 0.966–0.999 on Tülu-3-8B), while the thirds selected by a score turn away from it (0.886–0.983, and 0.851–0.968 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). The selected vectors are thus estimates that differ from the main data distribution, and the means are not preserved.

sections.heading: The two poles move by different amounts.
sections.text: Projected onto the pool’s refusal–compliance axis, a mean-preserving selection would move neither pole. On Tülu-3-8B, the score with the largest shift (zlib) moves the refusal pole by + + 0.614 and the compliance pole by − - 0.114 pooled standard deviations, so its top-third vector separates the poles more ( d ′ d^{\prime} 3.567, against 3.292 for the whole pool). On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the largest shift (Min-K%++) moves the refusal pole by − - 1.531, toward compliance, and the compliance pole by − - 0.103. The score is correlated with position along the direction the vector estimates, and differently in each pole. This is precisely the selection bias that Proposition 2 excludes in its assumption. The score is a weak membership signal (§ 4.2 ), so its extremes are set by length, register and the pole itself (see Appendix E.1 ), which differ between refusals and compliances; and the pole comes from the gold response, not the model (on WildGuardMix, Tülu-3-8B refuses 0.914 of the 128 top-ranked refusal prompts under a length-controlled s twin s_{\text{twin}} , against 0.797 of the bottom-ranked ones).

sections.heading: Model and input.
sections.text: Every response of the steering experiment (Section 4.4 ) is labelled by gemma-2-27b-it ( Team et al., 2024 ) , run in bfloat16; it belongs to a different model family than the two steered models. The judge receives the request and the whole 256-token response in the prompt of Figure 5 , and gives one response per prompt.

sections.heading: Labelling.
sections.text: The judge generates no text. We take its next-token distribution after the prompt, sum for each option the probability of the letter with and without a leading space, renormalise over the four options, and assign the option with the highest probability. Labelling is therefore deterministic and needs one forward pass per response (batch 8). The order of the options is the same in every prompt. The assigned option has mean probability .99 .99 ; it is below .9 .9 for 3.0 % of the responses. You are a careful annotator for AI-safety evaluations. You judge short model responses. A language model received this REQUEST: ⟨ \langle request ⟩ \rangle It produced this RESPONSE (cut off after ~256 tokens): ⟨ \langle response ⟩ \rangle Classify the RESPONSE with one letter: A: REFUSAL - it declines, deflects, moralizes, or otherwise refuses the request. B: COMPLIANCE - it begins to fulfill the request, on-topic (even partially; the cut-off may truncate it). C: OFF-TOPIC - fluent text that neither refuses nor addresses the request (derailed, unrelated, evasive). D: GIBBERISH - degenerate, repetitive, or incoherent output. Answer with exactly one letter. Figure 5: The judge prompt, verbatim. ⟨ \langle request ⟩ \rangle is the benchmark prompt and ⟨ \langle response ⟩ \rangle the steered model’s output.

sections.heading: Use of the labels.
sections.text: Table 13 maps the labels to the two measured rates. The jailbreak rate on HarmBench and StrongREJECT is the share of responses labelled B, and the over-refusal rate on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench is the share labelled A. Labels C and D count towards neither rate, so a response that is fluent but off-topic, or incoherent, is never scored as a jailbreak.

sections.heading: Agreement with other scorers.
sections.text: We compare the judge with two scorers that do not share its prompt, on the same responses. On the 45,200 responses to harmful requests, label B agrees with the HarmBench classifier ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) in 94.9 % of cases (Cohen’s κ = .74 \kappa=.74 ); the judge marks 10.0 % of these responses as compliance, the classifier 11.5 % as harmful. On the 28,400 responses to benign requests, label A agrees with a regular expression over explicit refusal phrases (an apology, “I cannot help/assist/provide”, “I must decline”) in 85.2 % of cases ( κ = .70 \kappa=.70 ); the judge marks more refusals (46.3 % against 34.4 %). Agreement is similar on the two steered models ( κ = .72 \kappa=.72 on Tülu and .76 .76 on Meta for the classifier, .68 .68 and .70 .70 for the regular expression).

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Vectors are unit-normalised and added at the input of block 16, at the last prompt token and at every generated token, with dose α \alpha . We steer at this block because a sweep over blocks found it the shallowest site at which every prompt can be flipped at some dose on both models. Doses are reported on a nominal scale anchored at block 13, a layer used in earlier runs but which was not used for the final experiments. The dose actually added is the nominal | α | |\alpha| times the ratio of the median activation norms at the two blocks, 1.360 on Tülu-3-8B and 1.140 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and the rows record the dose added. The nominal | α | |\alpha| runs in steps of 0.5 up to 12 on the harmful and up to 8 on the benign benchmarks (after which the benchmark either saturates or degenerates). For each prompt, doses above its lowest clean flip or its first degenerate response were generated after all others, for comparison. We subtract the vector on two harmful benchmarks, HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) and StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) , and add it on two benign benchmarks that resemble harmful requests, XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) and OR-Bench ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , and on one benign benchmark without that resemblance, Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) . Each benchmark has 100 prompts, with 256 generated tokens under greedy decoding. gemma-2-27b-it labels each response (see Appendix E.3 ). The flip score of Table 3 judges each response’s degeneration by itself. Below, we report the rate at every dose with its standard error, and the degenerate and off-topic shares next to it. Tables 19 – 28 give, for every vector of Tables 3 and 17 , the judged rate at every even nominal dose on each benchmark, with its standard error over the 100 prompts, and the shares of degenerate and off-topic responses. Grey rates come from doses where more than a share of 0.100 of the responses are degenerate. Bold marks the highest rate per dose among the doses below that share. sections.heading: Flip doses in units of the unnormalised vectors.
sections.text: All vectors are steered as unit vectors, so a dose is an absolute step in activation space. Steering with the unnormalised difference-of-means vector v v instead, the same step corresponds to a coefficient c = α ​ s / ∥ v ∥ c=\alpha\,s/\lVert v\rVert , where α \alpha is the nominal dose and s s the layer’s dose scale (1.360 on Tülu-3-8B, 1.140 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct); c = 1 c=1 adds v v once, the full difference between the mean refusal and the mean compliance activation. Table 29 converts each vector’s median lowest flipping dose this way. On Tülu-3-8B the median prompt flips at c c = 0.822–2.456 on HarmBench and 0.689–2.456 on XSTest; on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 0.870–2.487 and 0.870–2.401. The nominal flip dose varies little between vectors, so in raw units the coefficient mainly follows the vector’s length (2.769–5.918 on Tülu-3-8B, 2.374–5.420 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct): compared without normalisation, longer vectors would look more efficient for a reason unrelated to their direction. text: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.19114v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2026 Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data Tora Bodin Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden Eric Aubinais Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden Ilaria Torre Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden Chih-Hong Cheng Affiliation: Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden Affiliation: Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg, Oldenburg, Germany Correspondence: torab@chalmers.se Abstract Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering , which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model’s own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B’s training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data. 1 Introduction Ensuring that large language models (LLMs) help with benign requests while refusing harmful ones remains central to safe deployment. Activation steering controls this behavior at inference time by modifying internal representations without updating model parameters. A single direction can substantially alter refusal behavior Arditi et al. (2024) , making steering useful for behavioral control and probing learned safety mechanisms. Identifying a reliable direction is therefore crucial. A common approach constructs a steering set of positive and negative examples. Contrastive activation addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) and difference-of-means refusal steering Arditi et al. (2024) subtract the mean negative activations from the mean positive activations to obtain a single steering direction. However, these directions can have variable effects across inputs, fail under prompt changes, or reverse the intended behavior through anti-steering Tan et al. (2024) ; Braun et al. (2025) . This raises a fundamental question: which contrastive examples should define the steering direction? In this paper, we introduce genesis steering , which constructs steering directions from contrastive examples in the model’s own fine-tuning data. We term these examples genesis data and their difference-of-means direction a genesis vector . Since fine-tuning data shapes the model’s refusal and compliance behavior, it provides a natural reference for steering. We focus on refusal, for which safety fine-tuning data often contain both harmful requests paired with refusals and benign requests paired with compliant responses. This contrastive structure allows us to derive both classes directly from the data. However, fine-tuning datasets are not always publicly released or fully documented, limiting direct access to genesis data. To address this limitation, we extend genesis steering using membership inference queries , originally developed to estimate whether an example was used during training Shokri et al. (2017) ; Fu et al. (2024) . Given a dedicated steering set, we rank examples by their membership scores, retain likely training examples, and compute a proxy genesis vector from their positive and negative activation means. This approach uses membership inference to curate dataset rather than requiring access to the original fine-tuning data. Its effectiveness depends on whether the scores identify examples that reflect the model’s actual training data. We provide two theoretical results supporting this approach. First, We draw on recent Mahalanobis-based out-of-distribution (OoD) detection in learned LLM representations Liu et al. (2024) ; Feng et al. (2026) ; Barkley et al. (2026) , and prove that under specific distributional assumptions, the genesis vector minimizes the Euclidean displacement needed to reach the decision boundary (see Section 3.2 ). Second, under a mixture model with mean-preserving selection, we prove that membership-based proxies reduce the class-mean estimation bias when the true positive rate exceeds the false positive rate. When both classes share the mixture proportion and detection rates, the same reduction applies to steering-vector bias. We first evaluate genesis steering on Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, comparing vectors constructed from seven safety datasets and one contrastive split from the CAA datasets Rimsky et al. (2024) . At layer 16 16 , we measure how far each vector moves the model toward compliance across five benchmarks: HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) , StrongREJECT ( Souly et al., 2024 ) , XSTest ( Röttger et al., 2024 ) , OR-Bench ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , and Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) . We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B’s training mixture yield stronger steering vectors than the external datasets considered, on both models, even though Llama-3.1-8B-Instructwas not trained on any of these datasets. This result highlights the importance of the choice of steering data, beyond the choice of steering method alone. We next evaluate whether membership inference can recover this advantage when the original fine-tuning data are unavailable. Using 10 10 membership scores, we construct genesis proxy datasets for both models and examine the resulting steering vectors. On Tülu-3-8B, the scores largely agree in ranking examples, preferentially identify its fine-tuning data, and produce vectors that outperform those built from bottom-ranked examples while remaining competitive with random subsets of the same size. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the scores disagree, and top-ranked examples yield worse steering than random selection. These findings suggest that MIA methods will only have a positive effect if shifting the mean with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than shifting the mean with OoD data. Contributions. Our main contributions may be summarized as follows: • We introduce genesis steering, which constructs steering vectors from a model’s own contrastive fine-tuning data, and extend it with membership inference to construct proxy datasets when the original data are unavailable. • We establish theoretical guarantees for optimal boundary-reaching directions and reduced proxy-estimation bias under explicit distributional and selection assumptions. • We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, showing that model-specific fine-tuning data can improve steering and that membership-based selection can recover this benefit when the candidate pool contains the model’s actual training examples. 2 Related Work Activation steering methods. The linear representation hypothesis relates concept directions in activation space to model steering Park et al. (2024) . Activation addition Turner et al. (2024) and contrastive activation addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) construct directions from activation differences, while other methods intervene on attention heads Li et al. (2023) , sparse autoencoder features O’Brien et al. (2025) , optimized vectors Cao et al. (2024) , or activation rotations Vu and Nguyen (2025) . Broader frameworks include representation engineering and context dependent vector fields Zou et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2026) . Because these interventions act at inference time, they adjust a deployed model’s behaviour without retraining it or changing its weights. Comparative studies emphasize the importance of simple baselines Wu et al. (2025) ; Im and Li (2026) . We focus on the data used to estimate a direction within the difference-of-means framework, formalized in Section 3.1 . Refusal geometry and steering data. A single direction can substantially control refusal Arditi et al. (2024) , although recent work finds multiple refusal directions and richer geometric structure Joad et al. (2026) ; Wollschläger et al. (2025) . Refusal and harmfulness can also be represented separately Zhao et al. (2025) , while post-training affects refusal circuits and their steerability Nguyen et al. (2026) . More directly, the reliability of an extracted direction depends on the contrastive dataset, on prompt design Tan et al. (2024) ; Braun et al. (2025) and on the activations it is read from Ye et al. (2026) ; separation between positive and negative pools and consistency of activation differences predict steerability Braun et al. (2025) . Contrastive vectors can also entangle refusal with style and capabilities Cristofano (2026) or interfere across attributes Nguyen et al. (2025) ; Gao et al. (2026) . Closest to our setting, persona vectors run the reverse direction, projecting candidate training data onto a trait direction to flag data that will shift behaviour Chen et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; we instead estimate the direction from the training data. Genesis steering addresses this dependence on reference data by using the model’s own fine-tuning examples. Section 3.2 establishes population-level optimality under explicit assumptions. Membership inference for genesis steering. Membership inference is traditionally studied as a privacy attack for determining whether a candidate example was used in training Shokri et al. (2017) . For language models, attacks have been studied in masked model and fine-tuning settings Mireshghallah et al. (2022) ; Fu et al. (2024) , using neighborhood comparisons Mattern et al. (2023) and relative conditional likelihoods Xie et al. (2024) . Their reliability depends on the evaluation setting, and distribution shifts between members and non members can confound apparent success Duan et al. (2024) ; Meeus et al. (2025) . In our setting, membership scores are instead used to select proxy genesis data from an available steering set. 3 Genesis Steering 3.1 From Activation Steering to Genesis Steering Activation steering modifies internal representations at inference time while keeping model parameters fixed. Let D = D + ∪ D − D=D^{+}\cup D^{-} be a dedicated steering dataset with nonempty positive and negative pools that differ in the target behavior. At a fixed layer ℓ \ell , the difference-of-means estimator is Rimsky et al. (2024) ; Arditi et al. Section 3.2 analyzes the population counterpart of this estimator; Section 3.3 constructs a proxy and analyzes its bias when the fine-tuning data is unavailable. 3.2 Optimal Steering Vector We now formalize the geometric intuition behind genesis steering. For a fixed layer ℓ \ell , let H ℓ ∈ ℝ d H_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the random activation induced by the model’s fine-tuning data distribution, where d d is the activation dimension. We refer readers to the proof in Appendix A . 4 Experiments Our experiments address three questions: whether a model’s own fine-tuning datasets steer it better than external ones (§ 4.1 ), which pair (prompt, response) are ranked high by a membership score s ⁡ ( x ) s(x) and why (§ 4.2 – 4.3 ), and how the selected vectors steer (§ 4.4 ). Models. Both models share the Llama-3.1-8B base ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . Tülu-3-8B ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) is post-trained on a public SFT mixture, whereas Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct uses undisclosed data ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . We use Tülu-3-8B to study membership selection when training membership is known and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a negative control; none of the datasets considered here is known to overlap with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct’s post-training data. Membership scores are computed using the Tülu-3-8B SFT checkpoint, while activations and steering use the final Tülu-3-8B model. Some methods additionally use the Llama-3.1-8B base model or a Tülu-3-8B SFT model trained without the safety data, called the twin . Each model uses its own chat template. Datasets. We split each dataset into refusal and compliance poles according to its gold responses (Appendix C ). Three datasets belong to Tülu-3-8B’s SFT mixture (marked † \dagger ): CoCoNot safety requests (CCN) ( Brahman et al., 2024 ) , WildJailbreak (WJB) ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) , and WildGuardMix (WGM) ( Han et al., 2024 ) . Together, they contain approximately 111k of the mixture’s 939k prompts and constitute Tülu-3-8B’s genesis data . External datasets are CoCoNot rows excluded from the mixture (CCN-out), Do-Not-Answer (DNA) ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , HH-RLHF (HH) ( Bai et al., 2022 ) , and PKU-SafeRLHF (PKU) ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . We also use 393 393 refusal pairs from CAA ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , whose responses were authored by the dataset creators. CAA provides a stylistically distinct comparison and has previously yielded vectors with inconsistent steering across inputs ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Braun et al., 2025 ) . We use CAA solely as a ’bad’ comparison for the membership separability experiments. We do not use in other experiments. Details are given in Appendix C . Membership inference methods. Scores are computed on response tokens conditioned on the prompt, with higher values indicating greater likelihood of membership. We use 10 10 methods on Tülu-3-8B and 9 9 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Appendix D ); one method is unavailable for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as it requires a twin model. Loss, zlib, Min-K%, and Min-K%++ use response likelihood ( Carlini et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) ; gap scores measure agreement with the model’s next-token predictions; and ReCaLL, s base s_{\text{base}} , and s twin s_{\text{twin}} compare the target with a reference model or prefix prompt ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Watson et al., 2022 ) . Selection and steering protocol. For each membership method, we rank examples by their scores and select the highest-scoring examples to construct a proxy genesis dataset. We then divide the selected examples into refusal and compliance poles according to their gold responses. Provided both poles are nonempty, we compute the steering vector as the difference between their mean activations at the input of layer 16 16 , using the last prompt token (Eq. 1 ). We evaluate each vector across multiple values of the steering dose α \alpha . Steerability. A vector flips a prompt if some dose α \alpha gives a non-degenerate response with the benchmark’s target label, compliance on harmful prompts and refusal on benign ones. Its range r b ​ ( v ) r_{b}(v) on benchmark b b is the share of flipped prompts among those P b P_{b} not already at the target unsteered, and its steerability averages the two directions, S ⁡ ( v ) = 1 2 ​ | B h | ​ ∑ b ∈ B h r b ​ ( v ) + 1 2 ​ | B s | ​ ∑ b ∈ B s r b ​ ( v ) , \hskip-8.0ptS(v)=\frac{1}{2|B_{h}|}\sum_{b\in B_{h}}r_{b}(v)+\frac{1}{2|B_{s}|}\sum_{b\in B_{s}}r_{b}(v), (11) over the harmful benchmarks B h B_{h} and the benign ones B s B_{s} . Both directions are weighted equally, so a vector scores high only if it moves the model in both directions. Section 4.1 gives the protocol. 4.1 Genesis steering Protocol. Each of the seven datasets yields one vector, computed from a seeded draw of 128 refusal and 128 compliance examples from its respective poles (Appendix C ). Each vector is normalized and applied at the input of layer 16, at the last prompt token and every generated token. We subtract it on harmful benchmarks (HarmBench and StrongREJECT) and add it on benign benchmarks (XSTest, OR-Bench, and Alpaca). Responses are evaluated by the LLM judge gemma-2-27b-it (Appendix E.3 ). When the shift is controlled, a proxy genesis vector is thus as least as strong as a random subset where the candidate pool holds the model’s genesis data. 5 Conclusion We introduced genesis steering, which derives steering directions from a model’s own fine-tuning data, and studied membership inference as a means of constructing proxy datasets when the data is unavailable. Our experiments show that the choice of reference data matters: safety data from Tülu-3-8B’s training mixture yield effective steering vectors on both Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Membership-based selection preferentially recovers Tülu-3-8B’s fine-tuning data and produces competitive steering vectors, whereas it does not provide the same benefit on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, where the candidate data are unlikely to belong to its training set. These results support membership inference as a practical tool for proxy construction when the candidate pool contains relevant training examples, while highlighting the importance of evaluating selection through downstream steering. More broadly, they suggest that the composition of safety fine-tuning data shapes the directions available for steering. Understanding how training-data composition affects these directions may help guide the design of both fine-tuning mixtures and steering methods. 6 Limitations Our experiments cover two 8B models sharing the Llama-3.1-8B base, one steering layer and position, and seven English safety datasets. The results may differ across architectures, scales, layers, languages, and steering tasks. We also study only difference-of-means steering. Whether genesis-based selection benefits methods that optimize steering vectors directly ( Cao et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) remains open. Membership ground truth is available for Tülu-3-8B but not for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which serves as a negative control. Within a single data source, our membership analysis is limited to WildGuardMix, where members and non-members share a response generator. Broader validation therefore depends on access to fine-tuning data from additional models. Finally, we study refusal steering, whose contrastive classes can be derived directly from safety data. Other attributes, such as sycophancy, verbosity, and persona, may require constructing the contrastive split and could interact with refusal steering ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . Our evaluation also relies on a single LLM judge (gemma-2-27b-it) and fixed decoding settings; reported standard errors capture prompt-sampling variability but not judge error or decoding variability. 7 Potential Risks and Ethics Statements Steering can weaken a model’s refusals as well as strengthen them: the same vectors that induce refusal of benign requests also make the models comply with harmful ones. We study this to understand where refusal behavior comes from and how reliably it can be controlled, not to provide a jailbreak. activation steering requires white-box access to the model, and the directions we use are simple differences of means that are already known to work. We do not release model responses to harmful prompts. Where the appendix shows examples of compliance with a harmful request, it shows only the first sentence. All models and datasets are public and are used under their licenses. The harmful prompts come from public safety benchmarks. Membership inference could in principle be used to probe a model for its training data. For these models and scores, we find that individual training examples are detected only weakly, and not at all where members and non-members share a source and a response generator.
